newsitem.title: switzerland: UN says 300 Hutus killed in Burundi a month ago.
newsitem.headline: UN says 300 Hutus killed in Burundi a month ago.

text.p: The United Nations said on Friday 298 Burundian Hutus were killed just after they returned home from exile last month in an attack on a village church by men using guns and hand-grenades.

A human rights team which visited the Burundi province of Cibitoke on Thursday after hearing rumours of the incident learned for the first time at first hand of the massacre, which took place on the night of October 22-23, the U.N. said in Geneva.

Citing a report from the team, part of a seven-member human rights observer group in Burundi, the U.N. press service said 258 people died during the assault and 110 were wounded. Of these, 40 died later of their injuries.
The attackers used guns and hand-grenades to kill their victims in the Murambi church in Buganda commune.

Formal news of the killings was first given earlier on Friday by the U.N. refugee agency UNHCR, which said its special envoy to the region, Dessalegn Shefeke, was discussing the incident with the Burundian authorities.
Neither the UNHCR nor the human rights team's report alleged the Tutsi-dominated Burundian army -- accused of atrocities by Hutu exile groups -- was behind the killings.

But the U.N. report said human rights observers in Bujumbura, Burundi's capital, expressed serious concern to the local authorities there last week that returnees were being channelled into Cibitoke and Bubanza provinces.
In both areas, it said, "there is considerable confrontation between rebel forces and the government and humanitarian workers have extremely limited access".
Earlier on Friday, Burundi's prime minister, Pascal Firmin Ndimira, told reporters in Stockholm that his government could not be blamed for incidents like the Buganda killings.

"The government has no responsibility for this killing. It is non-uniformed rebels who would have done that," said Ndimira. U.N. officials and aid organisations were not always correctly informed, he added.
The U.N. said the victims were identified "as being among the large number of refugees who had recently returned of their own accord from exile in Zaire or Tanzania".
UNHCR spokeswoman Christiane Berthiaume said the dead were among some 3,000 Burundian Hutus who fled a Tutsi revolt in eastern Zaire and crossed to Cibitoke.

Diplomats in Geneva following the situation in central Africa said the massacre raised new questions over the forced return of Hutu refugees to Burundi and Rwanda -- where armies and governments are dominated by the Tutsi minority.

Some 35,000 Burundian Hutus have returned home from Zaire since the Tutsi rebellion there began a month ago. Another 500,000 Hutus from Rwanda have poured back into their country after Tutsi rebel shelling forced Hutu militiamen to flee.
The mass returns have pleased the UNHCR, which had tried unsuccessfully for two years to voluntarily repatriate them, as well as donors who paid $1 million a day to feed the refugees.
Before the latest crisis, U.S. and Western diplomats in the region privately advocated a forced but organised return.
Western aid agencies pulled out of Cibitoke in June after three Swiss staff members of the International Committee of the Red Cross were killed in an ambush.
At least 150,000 people have died in the past three years in Burundi's civil war after the country's first elected Hutu president was killed in an attempted coup by Tutsi soldiers.
